1.note: The book title is describing the messages that Isaiah received from Yahweh as if they were a single **vision** that he **saw**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The messages that Isaiah, the son of Amoz, received]

Here, **in the days of** represents the time period during which these kings reigned. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [during the reigns of]

1.q: חֲזוֹן֙ יְשַֽׁעְיָ֣הוּ בֶן־אָמ֔וֹץ אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָזָ֔ה עַל־יְהוּדָ֖ה וִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם בִּ⁠ימֵ֨י עֻזִּיָּ֧הוּ יוֹתָ֛ם אָחָ֥ז יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה׃
1.note: The word **Isaiah** is the name of a prophet and **Amoz** is the name of his father. The words **Uzziah**, **Jotham**, **Ahaz**, and **Hezekiah** are the names of kings of Judah. The words **Judah** and **Jerusalem** are the names of places. In your translation, here and in the rest of the book, represent names in the way that your language and culture naturally would.

2.note: Isaiah assumes that his listeners will understand that he is calling out to the heavens and the earth as witnesses to Yahweh’s covenant with the Israelites. (See Deuteronomy 4:6.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Hear, heavens, and listen, earth, you covenant witnesses]
The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before.

Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Israel were his **sons** whom he had raised and brought up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have helped and guided the people of Israel as a father raises his sons]

The terms **raised** and **brought up** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I have reared]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they have rebelled** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize the contrast between what he did for the Israelites and how they responded. Alternate translation: [but for their part, they have rebelled]

3.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and a donkey knows the manger of its master]

Here, the **manger** or feeding trough represents the **master** feeding the **donkey**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and a donkey recognizes who feeds it]

3.q: יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לֹ֣א יָדַ֔ע עַמִּ֖⁠י לֹ֥א הִתְבּוֹנָֽן
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Decide as a team how you will translate parallel phrases in this book in various contexts, and follow those approaches here and throughout your translation. Alternate translation: [Israel does not know; no, my people do not understand] or [my Israelite people do not respect me]

4.note: Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express a strong feeling of grief and judgment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Isaiah was feeling, or you could say what made him grieve. Alternate translation: [How awful]

The phrases **A sinning nation** and **a people heavy of iniquity** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [A very sinful people]

Yahweh is speaking as if the **iniquity** of the Israelites were actually **heavy**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who commit great iniquity]

Isaiah is speaking as if the descendants of evildoers were their **seed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [offspring of evildoers]

Isaiah is speaking as if the people of Israel were **sons** in a family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of mine who act corruptly]

Isaiah is speaking as if rejecting Yahweh were physically **turning away backward**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have rejected him]

Isaiah is using the adjective **Holy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of being. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **One**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. This title for Yahweh occurs frequently throughout the book, so decide how you will represent it consistently in your translation. Alternate translation: [the Holy God of Israel]

5.note: Isaiah is using the question form to rebuke the people for their continued sinning. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is nowhere on your body where you have not been struck.]

The expression **be struck** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will you still receive a blow]

Isaiah is using the question form to rebuke the people for their stubbornness. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You must not continue rebellion!]

Isaiah is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were a living thing that had a **head** that could experience **sickness** and a **heart** that could **faint**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

6.note: Isaiah is referring to all of the body by naming two major components, the **sole of the foot** and the **head**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [From the whole body]

6.q: אֵֽין־בּ֣⁠וֹ מְתֹ֔ם פֶּ֥צַע וְ⁠חַבּוּרָ֖ה וּ⁠מַכָּ֣ה טְרִיָּ֑ה
6.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the consequences of Israel’s sin were physical injuries such as a **Wound**, a **bruise** and a **raw sore**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no health in the people; they are full of injuries and suffering]

Isaiah is referring to all kinds of injuries by listing different types, **wound** and **bruise** and **raw sore**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Every kind of wound and sore]

6.q: לֹא־זֹ֨רוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א חֻבָּ֔שׁוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א רֻכְּכָ֖ה בַּ⁠שָּֽׁמֶן
6.note: The expressions **been pressed out**, **been bound up**, and **been softened** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one has pressed them out, no one has bound them up, and no one has softened them with oil]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is deserted]

Isaiah is speaking as if the destruction of the land was from the **strangers** **devouring** it like food. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [strangers are destroying it]

7.q: לְ⁠נֶגְדְּ⁠כֶם֙ זָרִים֙ אֹכְלִ֣ים אֹתָ֔⁠הּ וּ⁠שְׁמָמָ֖ה כְּ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֥ת זָרִֽים
7.note: The point of this comparison is that just as the **overthrow of strangers** is complete and devastating, so is the desolation of Israel’s land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it is as completely devastated as a land overthrown by strangers]

8.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **the daughter of Zion** to represent the city of Jerusalem and her inhabitants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the city of Jerusalem]

The expression **is left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has left Jerusalem]

8.q: כְּ⁠סֻכָּ֣ה בְ⁠כָ֑רֶם כִּ⁠מְלוּנָ֥ה בְ⁠מִקְשָׁ֖ה כְּ⁠עִ֥יר נְצוּרָֽה
8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a booth in a vineyard**, **a hut in a cucumber field**, and **a besieged city** are isolated and vulnerable, so is Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [standing alone]

9.q: לוּלֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת הוֹתִ֥יר לָ֛⁠נוּ שָׂרִ֖יד כִּ⁠מְעָ֑ט כִּ⁠סְדֹ֣ם הָיִ֔ינוּ לַ⁠עֲמֹרָ֖ה דָּמִֽינוּ
9.note: Isaiah is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. Yahweh of Armies did leave a remnant. He is stating it as a condition to show that Israel was not completely destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies has left us a remnant to survive, so we will not be destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah]

The point of this comparison is that just as **Sodom** and **Gomorrah** were completely destroyed, so would Israel have been destroyed without Yahweh’s intervention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Israel would have been destroyed]

10.note: By calling them **rulers of Sodom** and **people of Gomorrah**, Isaiah does not mean that they are literally from those cities. He means that the leaders and people of Judah are as wicked as the people of Sodom and Gomorrah were. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [wicked rulers like those of Sodom … wicked people like those of Gomorrah]

11.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people for bringing him so many sacrifices, which he does not desire. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The multitude of your sacrifices means nothing to me.]

11.q: וְ⁠דַ֨ם פָּרִ֧ים וּ⁠כְבָשִׂ֛ים וְ⁠עַתּוּדִ֖ים לֹ֥א חָפָֽצְתִּי
11.note: The phrase **the blood of bulls and lambs and male goats** is placed before the verb for emphasis. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the sacrifices before the information about Yahweh’s response. Alternate translation: [and I do not delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and male goats]

12.note: Here, **my face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my presence]

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people, meaning that no one asked them to come and trample his courts. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one has sought this from your hand, trampling my courts!]

The pronoun **this** refers to coming into Yahweh’s temple and trampling his courts. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [who has asked you to do this, trampling my courts]

Here, **your hand** represents the people’s initiative or agency. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from you]

13.note: Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe an **offering** that is characterized by **worthlessness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a worthless offering]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **worthlessness**, **abomination**, and **wickedness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [worthless things … is an abhorrent thing … wicked acts]

14.note: Yahweh is using the word **soul** to refer to his entire being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my whole being hates]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s festivals were a physical **burden** weighing him down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have become too much for me to bear]

The phrase **Your new moons and your annual festivals** is placed before the verb for emphasis. Your language may use similar emphasis strategies, or you may need to express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I hate your new moons and your annual festivals]

The expression **am wearied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [bearing them wearied me]

15.note: Spreading out the **palms** is a symbolic action that represents making a request to God in prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning of this action plainly. Alternate translation: [And when you pray to me]

Here, **my eyes** represents Yahweh’s attention and regard. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I turn my attention away from you]

Here, **blood** represents the guilt of violence and murder. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your hands are full of the guilt of violence and murder]

16.note: Here, **my eyes** represents Yahweh’s awareness and attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before my awareness]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people could **Wash** or **cleanse** themselves to remove their sin. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Get rid of your sins]

The terms **Wash** and **cleanse** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Really cleanse yourselves]

17.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just]

Isaiah is using the adjective **oppressed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [make glad those who have experienced oppression]

The phrase **gladden the oppressed** is one way to understand the consonants of the Hebrew text. The text can be read in another way as “rebuke the oppressor.” You may want to follow that reading in your translation, particularly if a translation of the Bible exists in your region and it follows that reading. Alternate translation: [rebuke the oppressor]

18.note: Yahweh is saying what he wants his people to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech, and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I would like us to argue together]

The point of this comparison is that just as **scarlet** is a deep stain that is difficult to remove, so the people’s sins seem irremovable, yet Yahweh promises to make them white like **snow**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Though your sins are as indelible as scarlet dye, they will become as pure as snow]

The point of this comparison is that just as **crimson** is a vivid, permanent dye, so the people’s sins seem indelible, yet Yahweh promises to make them as pure as **wool**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Thought they are as indelibly stained as crimson, they will become as white as wool]

20.note: The word translated as **If** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [In the event that you refuse and you rebel]

The expression **be devoured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the sword will devour you]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare and military destruction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you will be destroyed by warfare]
The phrase **for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken** closes Yahweh’s direct speech. In your translation, use a natural way of closing direct quotations in your language.

Isaiah is using one part of Yahweh, his **mouth**, to represent all of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself has spoken]

21.note: Isaiah is using the word **How** to express a strong feeling of grief and dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Isaiah was feeling, or you could say what made him grieve. Alternate translation: [It grieves me that the faithful city has become a prostitute]

Isaiah is speaking as if the city of Jerusalem were a **prostitute** who had abandoned faithful commitment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has become unfaithful]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is just; what is right]

Isaiah is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were a living thing that could **lodge** in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people acted righteously in her]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but now murderers dwell in her]

22.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the people of Jerusalem were **silver** that has degraded into **dross** or the scum of impurities. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You who were once pure have become corrupt]

Isaiah is speaking as if the quality of the people were **wine** that has been **diluted with water**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your people have become weak and worthless]

The expression **diluted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone has diluted your wine with water]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [your wine has become diluted with water]

23.note: The expression **each of him** uses a singular pronoun to refer to each individual among the princes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [every one of them]

24.q: נְאֻ֤ם הָֽ⁠אָדוֹן֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֲבִ֖יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
24.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to Isaiah. The phrase indicates that this is a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh declares]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [I will be relieved of my adversaries; indeed, I will be avenged of my enemies]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4.

25.note: Here, **my hand** represents Yahweh’s power and action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will use my power against you]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s impurities were **dross** that he will **refine**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will purify you of your impurities, and I will remove all of your corruption]

26.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will restore your counselors as they were at the beginning]

The expression **will be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will call it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Right Actions]

27.note: The expression **will be redeemed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will redeem Zion]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will save her repentant ones by righteousness]
See how you translated the similar expressions in 1:21.

28.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Transgressors and sinners will be destroyed together]

The terms **transgressors** and **sinners** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [those who sin greatly]

29.q: כִּ֣י יֵבֹ֔שׁוּ מֵ⁠אֵילִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר חֲמַדְתֶּ֑ם וְ⁠תַ֨חְפְּר֔וּ
29.note: The pronoun **they** in the first clause refers to the same people as **you** in the rest of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

29.q: מֵ⁠אֵילִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר חֲמַדְתֶּ֑ם & מֵ⁠הַ⁠גַּנּ֖וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּחַרְתֶּֽם
29.note: Here, **oaks** and **gardens** represent the places of idol worship associated with them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the oak trees where you desired to worship idols … from the gardens where you chose to worship idols]

30.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **an oak** with a **leaf withering** is losing its vitality, so the people will lose their strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you will lose vitality like an oak tree with withering leaves]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a garden** without water dries up and produces nothing, so the people will become unfruitful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a garden with no water, which dries up and produces nothing]

31.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the strong person were **tow** and his work were **a spark** that would ignite it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the strong man will become like kindling, and the work he has done will be like the spark that sets him on fire]

Isaiah is using the adjective **strong** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the strong person]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his work will be like a spark that sets him ablaze]
